opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to cost and risk. Pre-training is an enormously expensive undertaking. When you're committing thousands of accelerators for weeks or months, you really can't afford to bet the whole run on an untested idea. So the way teams work is very methodical: you run scaling studies on smaller models, you validate that a change holds up across several scales, and only then do you fold it into the big run. That naturally leads to incremental progress. You might change the data mixture, tweak the architecture a bit, improve the optimizer or stability tricks, but each of those has to earn its place through careful ablations.

There's also the fact that the core recipe for pre-training has been remarkably robust. Next-token prediction on a large, high-quality corpus with a transformer just works, and it keeps working as you scale. When something works that well, the highest-leverage improvements tend to be in the details: better data filtering, better deduplication, longer context, more efficient parallelism. Those are real gains, but they look incremental from the outside.

Post-training is a different world. The compute cost is much smaller relative to pre-training, so the iteration loop is much faster. You can try a new idea, whether it's a new reward modeling approach, a different way of doing reinforcement learning, synthetic data generation, or training the model to reason over longer chains of thought, and you can see the results in days rather than months. That lets people take bigger swings.

And the objectives themselves are more open-ended. In post-training you're shaping behavior: instruction following, safety, tool use, reasoning, being helpful in a conversation. There isn't a single settled recipe for that the way there is for pre-training, so there's a lot more room for qualitatively new approaches. We've seen that with the shift from pure supervised fine-tuning to RLHF, and then to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for things like math and code, which unlocked pretty dramatic changes in capability.

So I'd say pre-training builds this very strong foundation of knowledge and representations, and it evolves carefully because the stakes are high. Post-training is where you unlock and steer what that foundation can do, and because it's cheaper and less settled, that's where you see the more radical shifts happening right now.

r001.rationale: It describes testing changes on smaller models and validating them across scales, but does not say experience pre-training multiple model generations is needed to judge which changes to bet on.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training is enormously expensive and teams cannot afford to bet a large run on an untested idea, which encourages methodical, incremental changes.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that substantial pre-training changes can shift effort toward debugging instead of obtaining a working model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I think it comes down to a few things. The first is just cost. Pre-training is this enormous, expensive, months-long process. When you're spending that much compute, you're not going to take wild bets on the recipe. You iterate on data mixtures, you tweak the architecture a little, you scale up, but fundamentally the objective, next-token prediction on a huge corpus, has been remarkably stable. The scaling laws told us that if you do the boring thing well, you get predictable improvements, and that predictability is really valuable when the experiment costs tens of millions of dollars.

Post-training is the opposite in almost every way. It's cheap relative to pre-training, the iteration cycles are short, so you can try many ideas, and you can actually afford to be wrong. And I think the other piece is that post-training is where the objective is still genuinely unsettled. With pre-training, we know what we're optimizing for. With post-training, we're asking: what does it mean for a model to be helpful, to reason well, to follow instructions, to be safe? Those are much fuzzier targets, so the methods keep changing as our understanding changes. We went from supervised fine-tuning, to RLHF, to things like DPO, to reasoning-focused RL with verifiable rewards, and each of those felt like a real shift in how we think about the problem, not just a tweak.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that post-training is where most of the user-visible behavior lives. A pre-training improvement might show up as a couple of points on a benchmark, but a post-training change can completely transform how the model feels to interact with. So there's a lot of incentive to experiment there, and the feedback loop is much tighter. You see the effect right away. So I think it's really that combination: cost, maturity of the objective, and how quickly you can learn from what you tried.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training is an enormous, expensive process and that teams avoid wild bets when an experiment costs tens of millions of dollars, clearly linking the capital at stake to incremental changes.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it comes down to the cost of experimentation. In pre-training, you’re making a very large investment, and you want to understand which changes will reliably improve the model before you commit to a full run. So even when you have a promising idea, you typically validate it at smaller scales and build confidence. That naturally favors more incremental changes to the recipe.

Post-training gives you a much shorter feedback loop. You’re starting with a model that already has a broad set of capabilities, and you’re asking how to shape those capabilities into behavior that’s useful. You can experiment with different data, objectives, and ways of providing feedback at a fraction of the cost of pre-training. And relatively small changes there can produce very noticeable differences in how the model responds.

There’s also a difference in what we can measure. In pre-training, you have a fairly consistent objective, but improvements in that objective don’t always translate directly into an obvious change for a user. In post-training, you’re much closer to the interaction itself—whether the model follows instructions, solves a problem, or knows when to ask a clarifying question. So the changes can both happen faster and feel more radical.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how quickly you can iterate and how clear the learning signal is. In pre-training, you’re making a very large investment in compute and data. You can do smaller experiments, but ultimately you need to validate that an idea works at scale. That makes the feedback loop slower, and it encourages changes that you can reliably predict will improve the model.

Post-training gives you a much shorter feedback loop, and it lets you be more targeted about the behavior you want. You can change the data, the reward, or the training procedure and see a meaningful difference in how the model responds. Particularly in domains where you can verify an answer, reinforcement learning gives you a way to explore beyond simply imitating examples.

But I wouldn’t separate the two too sharply. Post-training is building on capabilities that pre-training made possible. Sometimes what looks like a radical change in behavior is a new way of drawing out or developing those underlying capabilities. The interesting question is how we make those two stages work together.

r001.rationale: It says pre-training ideas need validation at scale and favors predictable improvements, but does not say experience across multiple model generations is needed to judge which changes to pursue.

r002.rationale: It links the large investment in pre-training compute and data, and its slower feedback loop, to favoring changes expected to improve the model reliably.

r003.rationale: It does not say substantial pre-training changes divert effort into debugging instead of producing a working model.
